I should be honest: I know nothing about any of this, really. All I know is that Yann Lecun is a strong critic of LLMs as capable of achieving intelligence compared to world models, etc. Does this validate his criticism, or is this sleight of hand?

My answer is: this paper gives Yann LeCun some genuine ammunition, but it does not prove his central criticism of LLMs. And there is a bit of sleight of hand in how the findings are presented.
I wouldn't call the research fraudulent or meaningless. There is a real, interesting result here. But the distance between what the researchers demonstrated and what the headline invites you to believe is considerable.
The most important distinction is this:
The paper shows that one approach to training AI is better at learning a particular kind of representation of the world. It does not show that this approach is better at achieving intelligence.
Those sound similar, but they are very different claims.

First, the test favors the skill the researchers trained for. They're asking whether systems organize visual and textual descriptions similarly, and they've developed a method that explicitly teaches systems to recognize shared meaning across descriptions.
That's a perfectly legitimate research objective. But beating an LLM on this test is not equivalent to beating it at reasoning, scientific discovery, mathematics, or general intelligence.
Second, the successful model benefited from visual knowledge supplied by another AI. Much of its training text was generated by an existing image-understanding system. So although the new model never directly processed images, some of the knowledge it learned came from an AI that did.
This doesn't invalidate the controlled experiments. But it substantially weakens the more dramatic suggestion that the model independently discovered a representation of physical reality through text alone. The authors acknowledge this limitation on page 15. 
Third, the paper presents conditional mathematical results as though they settle a much broader question. The proof works under restrictive assumptions that the actual experiments do not fully satisfy. And the celebrated 42-fold efficiency advantage is a comparison of training samples at two endpoints—not a demonstrated 42-fold improvement in general computational efficiency.
Those are meaningful qualifications, even though the underlying findings are valuable.

I think LeCun has a serious and scientifically interesting criticism of relying exclusively on next-token prediction as the route to intelligence.
This paper supports one part of that criticism: predicting words is not necessarily the most efficient way to learn useful, shared representations of the world.
That's significant.
But I also think the paper's framing is more ambitious than its evidence warrants. Its authors have shown an advantage in representation learning and connected it to a much larger argument about intelligence, without establishing that larger argument.
It's not simply a trick. It's legitimate research presented with a substantial amount of rhetorical ambition. And because it was released on October 29, 2026—just yesterday—it has not yet had the benefit of sustained independent scrutiny.
There is one deeper question that I think sits at the heart of this entire disagreement:
If an AI can accurately reason about the world, predict events, solve novel problems, and make successful plans, does it matter whether it learned those abilities by predicting words or by building the kind of internal world model LeCun advocates?
My view is that the abilities themselves have to be the ultimate test. A theory about how intelligence ought to be learned is not enough to establish which systems can actually achieve it.
